title: SQLite WAL mode for application teams
topic: How SQLite write-ahead logging (WAL) mode works for an application team deciding whether to enable it: reader/writer interaction, checkpoints, durability and limitations
scope: How SQLite's write-ahead logging (WAL) journal mode works, for an application team deciding whether to enable it: reader/writer concurrency, checkpoints, durability and crash recovery, and limitations. Public sources, sqlite.org documentation first; current documentation as of October 2026.
prose_review: not independently reviewed at light depth

questions.question: In WAL mode, do readers and writers block each other, and what does a reader see while a write is in progress?

headline.sentence: In WAL mode readers and writers ordinarily do not block each other, and each read transaction sees a fixed snapshot of the database as of the last commit before it started.

answer.sentence: In WAL mode, changes are appended to a separate WAL file and a transaction commits when a commit record is appended there, so committing need not write the original database file and readers can keep using it unaltered.
As a result, readers ordinarily do not block writers and a writer does not block readers, so reading and writing can generally proceed concurrently.
By contrast, rollback mode must temporarily expel all readers before a writer changes the database file on disk.
When a read transaction starts, it fixes an "end mark" at the last valid commit record, so it sees the database as of a single point in time.
For each page, the reader uses the last copy in the WAL before its end mark, or otherwise the page in the database file, and it locates WAL pages through a shared-memory wal-index.
That shared-memory wal-index is why all readers must be on the same machine.
The result is snapshot isolation: write transactions that commit while a read transaction is open stay invisible to that reader.
To see changes another connection committed meanwhile, the reading connection must end its read transaction and begin a new one, for example with COMMIT then BEGIN.
A reader on a separate connection never sees a writer's uncommitted changes, unless both connections share a cache and the reader enables PRAGMA read_uncommitted.
The non-blocking behaviour has exceptions: queries can return SQLITE_BUSY when another connection uses exclusive locking mode, while the last connection cleans up, or during crash recovery.
During WAL recovery after a crash, exclusive locks stop other connections from writing or reading WAL transactions until recovery completes, so a concurrent query may get SQLITE_BUSY.
An operation that cannot continue because another process is recovering the database gets the extended code SQLITE_BUSY_RECOVERY, which SQLite returns only on WAL databases.
Readers also affect checkpoints: a checkpoint runs alongside readers but stops at pages past any current reader's end mark, so a long-running read transaction can stall checkpoint progress.
If many overlapping readers keep at least one read transaction always active, no checkpoint can complete or reset the WAL, and the WAL file grows without bound.
The WAL documentation says manual SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE checkpoints run to completion, but that readers might block while such a checkpoint runs.

SQLite's checkpoint API documentation qualifies that completion claim: if the busy handler returns 0 before a FULL, RESTART or TRUNCATE checkpoint gets the writer lock or while it waits for readers, the checkpoint continues like PASSIVE and returns SQLITE_BUSY.
Read together, these sources say a RESTART or TRUNCATE checkpoint might block readers while it runs but is not guaranteed to complete.

questions.question: How many writers can be active at once in WAL mode, and what happens when another connection tries to write?

headline.sentence: WAL mode allows only one writer at a time alongside any readers, and another connection that tries to start a write meanwhile gets SQLITE_BUSY and must wait for the first transaction to finish.

answer.sentence: WAL mode allows only one writer at a time because there is only one WAL file, although that writer runs alongside readers.
SQLite supports multiple simultaneous read transactions from separate connections, threads or processes, but only one simultaneous write transaction.
Many open connections may write to the database, but they take turns, with SQLite applying the locks automatically rather than the application.
When a second connection tries to start a write transaction while another write is underway, it gets SQLITE_BUSY and must wait for the first transaction to finish.
SQLite's default busy callback is NULL, so unless a handler or timeout is set, a connection gets SQLITE_BUSY immediately when it meets a lock.
SQLite offers sqlite3_busy_timeout(), sqlite3_busy_handler() and PRAGMA busy_timeout so that a connection blocked by another writer can handle SQLITE_BUSY by waiting and retrying.
The sqlite3_busy_timeout() handler sleeps repeatedly until at least the given number of milliseconds have accumulated, and then lets sqlite3_step() return SQLITE_BUSY.
A busy handler is not guaranteed to run: if invoking it could cause a deadlock, SQLite returns SQLITE_BUSY to the application instead.

Transactions default to DEFERRED, so a transaction that starts with SELECT is a read transaction, and a later write upgrades it only if no other connection has modified or is modifying the database; otherwise the write gets SQLITE_BUSY.
In WAL mode, a read transaction that tries to write after another connection has written fails with SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT and must release its snapshot and start a new transaction.

BEGIN IMMEDIATE instead starts a write transaction at once and blocks other writers; it may itself fail with SQLITE_BUSY, but once it succeeds, later statements in that transaction never fail with SQLITE_BUSY.
In WAL mode, BEGIN EXCLUSIVE behaves the same as BEGIN IMMEDIATE; only in other journal modes does EXCLUSIVE also stop other connections from reading.
This concurrency is limited to one host: all processes using a WAL database must be on the same host, so WAL does not work over a network filesystem.
For clients on several machines needing simultaneous reads and writes, SQLite suggests WAL only if all reads and writes run on the database machine, with a proxy relaying remote requests.

questions.question: What is a WAL checkpoint and when does SQLite run one automatically?

headline.sentence: A checkpoint moves WAL transactions back into the database file, and by default SQLite runs one when a COMMIT brings the WAL to 1000 pages or more, or when the last connection closes.

answer.sentence: A WAL checkpoint is the operation that moves transactions appended in the WAL file back into the original database file.
In WAL mode, changes are appended to the separate WAL file and a COMMIT occurs when a commit record is appended there, so committing need not write the original database.
Checkpoints sync the WAL before moving content into the database and sync the database before the WAL is reset, to avoid corruption after power loss or a hard reboot.
With synchronous=NORMAL in WAL mode, syncs happen around checkpoints and WAL reuse, but no sync operations occur during most transactions.
By default, SQLite runs a checkpoint automatically whenever a COMMIT makes the WAL file 1000 pages or more, or when the last connection on the database file closes.
That last connection normally runs a final checkpoint and deletes the -wal and -shm files, although the WAL may remain after an unclean exit or with SQLITE_FCNTL_PERSIST_WAL.
Once the WAL reaches about 1000 pages, the default strategy runs a checkpoint for each subsequent COMMIT until the WAL is reset to fewer than 1000 pages.
Normally the WAL is checkpointed at about 1000 pages, about 4MB, and then recycled by overwriting it from the beginning rather than truncated, unless journal_size_limit is set.
The default automatic checkpoint runs on the same thread as the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit, so occasional checkpoint-triggering COMMITs are much slower than most.
Automatic checkpoints are always PASSIVE: they do as much work as possible without interfering with other connections and might not run to completion when readers or writers are active.
Every new database connection starts with auto-checkpointing enabled at a threshold of 1000 pages, or at the value of the compile-time SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT option.
At run time, PRAGMA wal_autocheckpoint=N makes SQLite checkpoint automatically whenever the WAL equals or exceeds N pages, and a zero or negative value turns auto-checkpointing off.
Because sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint() is a wrapper around sqlite3_wal_hook(), registering a separate sqlite3_wal_hook() callback also disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism.

Applications can instead force checkpoints with PRAGMA wal_checkpoint or sqlite3_wal_checkpoint(), or disable automatic checkpoints and run them during idle moments or in a separate thread or process.
SQLite says that with synchronous=NORMAL and checkpoints run in a separate thread or process, the main thread never blocks on sync, but transactions are no longer durable across power failure.

Unlike the automatic checkpoints, which are always PASSIVE, a FULL checkpoint blocks via the busy handler until no writer is running and all readers use the latest snapshot, then checkpoints all frames.
A RESTART checkpoint additionally waits for readers to leave the log, and a TRUNCATE checkpoint additionally truncates the log to zero bytes on success.
SQLite pages disagree on whether RESTART and TRUNCATE checkpoints are guaranteed to complete, as set out in the answer on checkpoint starvation.

questions.question: What can prevent a checkpoint from completing or the WAL file from being reset, and what are the consequences?

headline.sentence: A long-running SQLite read transaction stops a checkpoint from completing or resetting the WAL, and constantly overlapping readers can make the WAL grow without bound, using excess disk space and slowing queries.

answer.sentence: A SQLite checkpoint can run alongside readers but must stop at any WAL page past a current reader's end mark, because continuing might overwrite database content that reader is using.
A checkpoint records its progress in the wal-index and resumes from there next time, so a long-running read transaction can stop the checkpointer from making progress.

While another connection holds a read transaction open, a checkpoint does what it can but cannot run to completion or reset the WAL, and it restarts where it left off after the next write transaction.

When a write occurs, the writer rewinds the WAL to its beginning if the entire WAL has been transferred into the database and synced and no readers are using the WAL, which is what prevents unbounded WAL growth.
In checkpoint starvation, many overlapping readers keep at least one read transaction always active, so no checkpoint can complete or reset the WAL and the WAL file grows without bound.
An unboundedly growing WAL causes excess disk space usage and slow queries, because each reader must check the WAL and that time is proportional to the WAL file's size.
The wal-index speeds finding pages in the WAL, but read performance still falls off as the WAL grows.
Writers can also keep the WAL from being reset: it cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction, so a very large write transaction can make the WAL grow very big until it completes.
Compile-time and run-time options can disable or defer the automatic checkpoint, and if an application disables it, nothing prevents the WAL file from growing excessively.
sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) checkpoints after a commit once the WAL has N or more frames, and passing zero or a negative N disables automatic checkpoints entirely.

The compile-time option SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT sets the default auto-checkpoint page count, otherwise 1000, and SQLITE_DEFAULT_JOURNAL_SIZE_LIMIT sets the WAL size limit, otherwise unbounded.
Automatic checkpoints are always PASSIVE, a mode that never invokes the busy handler and might leave the checkpoint unfinished when there are concurrent readers or writers.
Every checkpoint call needs an exclusive checkpoint lock, so a checkpoint attempted while another process is checkpointing returns SQLITE_BUSY without invoking the busy handler.

A checkpoint normally only overwrites the WAL from the beginning rather than truncating it, and journal_size_limit, whose default of -1 means no limit, truncates a larger leftover WAL at each commit or WAL reset.

For detection, PRAGMA wal_checkpoint returns 1 in its first column when a FULL, RESTART or TRUNCATE checkpoint was blocked from completing, for example by another thread or process using the database.
Its second column reports modified pages written to the WAL and its third column the WAL pages moved back into the database by the checkpoint, and both are -1 without a WAL.
sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() sets *pnLog to the total frames in the WAL and *pnCkpt to all checkpointed frames, including ones checkpointed before the call, or both to -1 on error or outside WAL mode.
The SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP mode always checkpoints zero frames and exists only to read those *pnLog and *pnCkpt values.

A sqlite3_wal_hook callback receives the number of pages currently in the WAL, including those just committed, and an application that sets one should periodically checkpoint to keep the WAL from growing without bound.
SQLite documentation says checkpoint starvation can be avoided by ensuring reader gaps, times when no process is reading the database, and attempting checkpoints during those gaps.
The documentation also says to keep the WAL small by running checkpoints at regular intervals.

For applications with many concurrent readers, the WAL documentation suggests considering manual RESTART or TRUNCATE checkpoints, which it presents as running to completion before returning, with the disadvantage that readers might block meanwhile.

A RESTART checkpoint works like FULL but also waits, via the busy handler, until all readers read only from the database file, so the next writer restarts the WAL; TRUNCATE also truncates it to zero bytes.

The sources disagree on whether that completion is guaranteed: the C checkpoint interface documentation says a FULL, RESTART or TRUNCATE checkpoint whose busy handler returns 0 continues like PASSIVE and returns SQLITE_BUSY.

sqlite3_busy_timeout installs a busy handler that sleeps until at least the given milliseconds accumulate and then returns 0, the value that makes a blocking checkpoint fall back to PASSIVE behaviour.

Read together, these pages mean a RESTART or TRUNCATE checkpoint waiting on an open reader can return SQLITE_BUSY without completing once its busy handler gives up, a block that PRAGMA wal_checkpoint reports as 1 in its first column.

questions.question: How durable is a committed transaction in WAL mode under synchronous=NORMAL compared with synchronous=FULL?

headline.sentence: In WAL mode, synchronous=FULL syncs the WAL on every commit and is documented as ACID, while under NORMAL, which skips that sync, a committed transaction might roll back after power loss or a system crash.

answer.sentence: With synchronous=FULL, SQLite syncs the WAL after every transaction commit, whereas synchronous=NORMAL omits that per-commit sync.
Under NORMAL, syncs still happen around checkpoints and WAL reuse, but no sync operations occur during most transactions.
SQLite documents FULL as atomic, consistent, isolated and durable (ACID) in WAL mode, unlike rollback-journal mode, where FULL is not necessarily durable across power loss.
The EXTRA level adds nothing over FULL in WAL mode, because its extra directory sync applies only to rollback journals in DELETE mode.
Under NORMAL, a committed transaction might roll back after a power loss or system crash, although the database stays consistent and safe from corruption.
SQLite's pragma documentation describes NORMAL as losing only durability across power loss, while keeping atomicity, consistency and isolation.
This loss does not cover application crashes, since SQLite documents transactions as durable across application crashes regardless of the synchronous setting or journal mode.
SQLite says that with NORMAL and checkpoints run in a separate thread or process, the main thread never blocks on sync, but transactions are no longer durable across power failure.
SQLite's pragma documentation calls NORMAL the best performance-safety balance for most WAL-mode applications.
SQLite's compile-options guide says transaction commit is much faster in WAL mode with NORMAL than with FULL, and recommends switching from FULL to NORMAL when moving to WAL.
Unless overridden at compile time, SQLite's default synchronous setting is 2 (FULL), and databases that open in WAL mode use that same default unless SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_SYNCHRONOUS is overridden.
SQLite cannot detect storage that lies about sync requests, and in WAL mode a failed sync during COMMIT can lose durability, while only a failed sync during a checkpoint can corrupt the database.

questions.question: What happens to committed and uncommitted transactions in the WAL after a crash or power loss?

headline.sentence: After a crash, the first connection runs WAL recovery, which sets the valid end of the WAL at the last valid commit frame so uncommitted frames are not read, provided the -wal file stays with the database.

answer.sentence: In WAL mode a transaction commits when a commit record is appended to the WAL, while the original content stays unmodified in the database file.
SQLite describes the -wal file as a roll-forward journal of committed but not-yet-applied transactions.
Checkpoints sync the WAL before moving content into the database and sync the database before resetting the WAL, to avoid corruption after power loss or a hard reboot.
After a crash, the first connection to the database runs recovery, a single pass over the WAL that verifies frame checksums and stops at the end of file or the first invalid checksum.
A frame is valid only if its salt values match the WAL header and its cumulative checksum matches, which lets SQLite separate valid frames from leftovers of earlier checkpoints.
Recovery sets the valid end of the WAL at the last valid commit frame, and readers use only page frames that are, or are followed by, a commit frame, so uncommitted frames are not read.
Because recovery cannot tell how many frames were already copied into the database, it initializes the nBackfill value to zero.
The -shm wal-index file holds no database content, is never fsynced, and is not required to recover the database after a crash.
SQLite documents committed transactions as durable across application crashes regardless of the synchronous setting or journal mode.
After a power loss or system crash, a committed transaction might roll back under synchronous=NORMAL, although the database stays consistent and safe from corruption.
Under synchronous=FULL, SQLite documents WAL mode as durable as well as atomic, consistent and isolated.
SQLite cannot detect storage that lies about sync requests, and in WAL mode a failed sync during COMMIT can lose durability, while only a failed sync during a checkpoint can corrupt the database.
When the last connection closes, it normally runs a final checkpoint and deletes the -wal and -shm files, but the WAL may remain after an unclean exit.
Moving, deleting or renaming such a hot WAL after a crash defeats automatic recovery and may corrupt the database.
SQLite says the WAL file is part of the database's persistent state and should be kept with it when copied or moved, since separating them might lose committed transactions or corrupt the database.
According to SQLite, the only safe way to remove a WAL file is to open the database with an sqlite3_open() interface and immediately close it with sqlite3_close().

While recovery runs, exclusive locks stop other connections from writing or reading WAL transactions, so a concurrent query may get SQLITE_BUSY, and SQLite returns the extended code SQLITE_BUSY_RECOVERY in that situation on WAL databases.

questions.question: Can WAL mode be used when the database is on a network filesystem or accessed from several machines, and why?

headline.sentence: Not over a network filesystem: SQLite says every process using a WAL database must be on the same host, because the processes must share memory.

answer.sentence: SQLite's WAL documentation says all processes using a WAL database must be on the same host, so WAL does not work over a network filesystem.
The shared memory in question is the wal-index, which WAL readers use to locate pages in the WAL, and it is why all readers must be on the same machine.
SQLite implements this wal-index shared memory by memory-mapping an ordinary file in the same directory as the database file.

For clients on several machines that need simultaneous reads and writes, SQLite's network guidance suggests WAL only if all reads and writes run on the database machine, with a proxy relaying the remote requests.
The same guidance also lists a client/server engine such as PostgreSQL, or SQLite in rollback mode, which allows simultaneous readers or one writer but not both.
SQLite says rollback mode can mitigate network unreliability, but SQLite is not tested across networks, so using a remote database file is at the user's risk.
It also warns that exclusive file locks on some network filesystems have operated incorrectly and led to database corruption, and that sync and locking reliability vary across networks.

questions.question: What other limitations does WAL mode have compared with rollback-journal mode (for example read-only access, very large transactions or ATTACHed databases)?

headline.sentence: Besides the same-host rule, SQLite documents WAL limits on cross-database atomicity with ATTACH, page-size changes, read-only access, extra -wal and -shm files, and reading by SQLite versions before 3.7.0.

answer.sentence: In WAL mode, a transaction that changes several ATTACHed databases is atomic for each database but not atomic across all the databases as a set.
A WAL-mode database's page_size cannot be changed, including by VACUUM or by restoring a backup; changing the page size requires a rollback journal mode.
SQLite versions before 3.7.0 cannot read a WAL-mode database, because WAL mode raises the file format version numbers in the header from 1 to 2.
Running PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE leaves WAL mode and changes those version numbers back to 1 so older SQLite versions can open the database.
Read-only access depends on the release: before SQLite 3.22.0, opening a WAL-mode database required write access to the -shm file or, if that file was absent, to the database's directory.
Since 3.22.0, a read-only WAL database can be read if the -shm and -wal files exist and are readable, if the directory is writable, or if the immutable parameter is used.
Even so, SQLite recommends converting a database to journal_mode=DELETE before putting it on read-only media.
WAL adds quasi-persistent -wal and -shm files beside each database, which SQLite says can make WAL less appealing as an application file format.

The WAL file is part of the database's persistent state and should be kept with the database when it is copied or moved, because separating them might lose committed transactions or corrupt the database.
WAL without shared memory works only if locking_mode is EXCLUSIVE before first access, and that connection then stays EXCLUSIVE until it leaves WAL mode.
In-memory databases can only use the MEMORY or OFF journal modes, so they cannot use WAL.
A WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction, so a very large write transaction can make the WAL grow very big until it completes.

The WAL page's large-transaction guidance is mixed: it says rollback modes are likely faster above about 100-megabyte transactions and recommended above a few dozen megabytes, yet says WAL works as efficiently with large transactions beginning with 3.11.0.
The page dates that 3.11.0 change to 2016-02-15.
Separately, WAL may be very slightly slower than rollback-journal mode, perhaps 1% or 2%, in applications that mostly read and seldom write.

questions.question: How is WAL mode enabled, and does the setting persist across connections and database closes?

headline.sentence: WAL is enabled by running PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL and, unlike other journal modes, it persists across connections and after the database is closed and reopened.

answer.sentence: SQLite connections default to journal_mode=DELETE, and a database is converted to WAL by running PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL.
The pragma returns "wal" on success; if conversion fails, for example because the VFS lacks shared-memory support, the mode is unchanged and the prior mode is returned.
Without a schema name, PRAGMA journal_mode changes the journal mode for all attached databases.
The journal mode cannot be changed while a transaction is active, and in-memory databases cannot use WAL because they can only use MEMORY or OFF.
Unlike other journal modes, WAL mode is persistent: it stays in effect across connections and after the database is closed and reopened.
By contrast, non-WAL modes such as TRUNCATE do not persist, and after closing and reopening the database returns to the default DELETE rollback mode.
Setting WAL journal mode on any one connection sets it on all connections to the same database file.
Because the setting persists, an application can be switched to WAL without code changes by running PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL with a utility and then restarting the application.
WAL mode is left explicitly by running PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE, which changes the file format version numbers back to 1 so older SQLite versions can open the database.
When the last connection closes, it normally runs a final checkpoint and deletes the -wal and -shm files, though the WAL may remain after an unclean exit or with SQLITE_FCNTL_PERSIST_WAL.
SQLite says the only safe way to remove a WAL file is to open the database with an sqlite3_open() interface and immediately close it with sqlite3_close().
If a connection is in EXCLUSIVE locking mode when it first enters WAL mode, it cannot switch to NORMAL locking until it exits WAL mode, whereas entering under NORMAL allows switching freely.

questions.question: What performance advantages and disadvantages does SQLite's documentation give for WAL compared with rollback-journal mode, and for which workloads?

headline.sentence: SQLite's documentation calls WAL significantly faster than a rollback journal in most scenarios, though perhaps 1% or 2% slower for applications that mostly read and seldom write.

answer.sentence: SQLite's WAL documentation says WAL is significantly faster than a rollback journal in most scenarios.
WAL write transactions are very fast because they write content once, versus twice for rollback-journal transactions, and all their writes are sequential.
SQLite also says disk I/O tends to be more sequential with WAL, and that WAL uses many fewer fsync() operations than a rollback journal, so it is less vulnerable where fsync() is broken.

For workloads mixing reads and writes, WAL gives more concurrency: readers and a writer proceed concurrently, whereas rollback mode temporarily expels readers before a writer changes the database file.
SQLite's compile-options guide says transaction commit is much faster in WAL mode with synchronous=NORMAL than with FULL.
For applications that mostly read and seldom write, SQLite says WAL might be very slightly slower than rollback-journal mode, perhaps 1% or 2%.
WAL read performance falls off as the WAL file grows, even with the wal-index, so SQLite advises checkpointing at regular intervals to keep the WAL small for good read performance.
Checkpoints are slower than write transactions because they require sync operations and more seeking, with many seeks typically interspersed among the page writes.
The default automatic checkpoint runs on the same thread as the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit, so occasional checkpoint-triggering COMMITs are much slower than most.

Checkpoint frequency trades reads against writes: frequent checkpoints, perhaps every COMMIT, maximize read performance, while infrequent checkpoints that let the WAL grow maximize write performance by amortizing checkpoint cost.

SQLite says its default checkpoint at 1000 pages seems to work well in test applications on workstations, but that checkpoint frequency may vary with each application's read and write needs, platform and workload.
Under synchronous=NORMAL the checkpoint is the only operation that issues a sync, so running it in a separate thread or process helps prevent latch-up on a busy disk drive.
SQLite adds that with synchronous=NORMAL and checkpoints in a separate thread or process, the main thread never blocks on sync, but transactions are no longer durable across power failure.
EXCLUSIVE locking mode reduces filesystem system calls, possibly giving a small performance increase, and with it WAL shared memory can come from heap rather than a -shm file.
On large transactions, the WAL page says that beginning with version 3.11.0 (2016-02-15), WAL mode works as efficiently with large transactions as does rollback mode.
The same page also says rollback modes are likely faster above about 100-megabyte transactions, a statement that sits beside the 3.11.0 note.

facts.statement: SQLite's WAL documentation says all processes using a WAL database must be on the same host, so WAL does not work over a network filesystem, because processes must share memory.

citations.quote: All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem. This is because WAL requires all processes to share a small amount of memory and processes on separate host machines obviously cannot share memory with each other.

facts.statement: WAL readers use a shared-memory wal-index to locate pages in the WAL, and that shared memory is why all readers must be on the same machine.

citations.quote: a data structure called the "wal-index" is maintained in shared memory which helps readers locate pages in the WAL quickly and with a minimum of I/O. The wal-index greatly improves the performance of readers, but the use of shared memory means that all readers must exist on the same machine. This is why the write-ahead log implementation will not work on a network filesystem.

facts.statement: SQLite implements the WAL wal-index shared memory by memory-mapping an ordinary file in the same directory as the database file.

citations.quote: The wal-index is implemented using an ordinary file that is mmapped for robustness.
citations.locator: 7. Implementation Of Shared-Memory For The WAL-Index

citations.quote: The only way we have found to guarantee that all processes accessing the same database file use the same shared memory is to create the shared memory by mmapping a file in the same directory as the database itself.
citations.locator: 7. Implementation Of Shared-Memory For The WAL-Index

facts.statement: For clients on several machines needing simultaneous reads and writes, SQLite suggests WAL only if all reads and writes run on the database machine, with a proxy relaying remote requests.

citations.quote: Network filesystems do not support the ability to do simultaneous reads and writes while at the same time keeping the database consistent. So if you have multiple clients on multiple different machines which need to do simultaneous database reads and writes, you have these choices:

Host an SQLite database in WAL mode, but do all reads and writes from processes on the same machine that stores the database file. Implement a proxy that runs on the database machine that relays read/write requests from remote machines.

facts.statement: SQLite says rollback mode can mitigate network unreliability, but SQLite is not tested across networks, so using a remote database file is at the user's risk.

citations.quote: These network unreliability issues can be mitigated, completely or to an acceptable degree, by using SQLite in rollback mode. However, the SQLite library is not tested in across-a-network scenarios, nor is that reasonably possible. Hence, use of a remote database is done at the user's risk.

facts.statement: SQLite warns that exclusive file locks on some network filesystems have operated incorrectly and led to database corruption, and that network sync and locking reliability vary.

citations.quote: A similar hazard arises with file locking in network filesystems. SQLite relies on exclusive locks for write operations, and those have been known to operate incorrectly for some network filesystems. This has led to database corruption.
The bottom line is that network filesystem sync and locking reliability vary among implementations and installations.

facts.statement: In WAL mode, a transaction changing multiple ATTACHed databases is atomic for each database but not atomic across all the databases as a set.

citations.quote: Transactions that involve changes against multiple ATTACHed databases are atomic for each individual database, but are not atomic across all databases as a set.

facts.statement: A WAL-mode database's page_size cannot be changed, including by VACUUM or backup restore; changing page size requires a rollback journal mode.

citations.quote: It is not possible to change the page_size after entering WAL mode, either on an empty database or by using VACUUM or by restoring from a backup using the backup API. You must be in a rollback journal mode to change the page size.

facts.statement: Before SQLite 3.22.0, opening a WAL-mode database required write access to the -shm file or, if absent, to the database's directory.

citations.quote: It is not possible to open read-only WAL databases. The opening process must have write privileges for "-shm" wal-index shared memory file associated with the database, if that file exists, or else write access on the directory containing the database file if the "-shm" file does not exist. Beginning with version 3.22.0 (2018-01-22), a read-only WAL-mode database file can be opened if the -shm and -wal files already exist or those files can be created or the database is immutable.

facts.statement: Since SQLite 3.22.0, a read-only WAL database can be read if the -shm and -wal files exist and are readable, the directory is writable, or the immutable parameter is used.

citations.quote: This constraint was relaxed beginning with SQLite version 3.22.0 (2018-01-22).
On newer versions of SQLite, a WAL-mode database on read-only media, or a WAL-mode database that lacks write permission, can still be read as long as one or more of the following conditions are met:
The -shm and -wal files already exist and are readable.
There is write permission on the directory containing the database so that the -shm and -wal files can be created.
The database connection is opened using the immutable query parameter.

facts.statement: SQLite recommends converting a database to journal_mode=DELETE before putting it on read-only media, even though read-only WAL databases can be opened.

citations.quote: Even though it is possible to open a read-only WAL-mode database, it is good practice to convert the database to PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE prior to burning an SQLite database image onto read-only media.

facts.statement: WAL may be very slightly slower than rollback-journal mode, perhaps 1% or 2%, in applications that mostly read and seldom write.

citations.quote: WAL might be very slightly slower (perhaps 1% or 2% slower) than the traditional rollback-journal approach in applications that do mostly reads and seldom write.

facts.statement: WAL adds quasi-persistent -wal and -shm files beside each database, which SQLite says can make it less appealing as an application file format.

citations.quote: There is an additional quasi-persistent "-wal" file and "-shm" shared memory file associated with each database, which can make SQLite less appealing for use as an application file-format.

facts.statement: A WAL-mode database cannot be read by SQLite versions before 3.7.0, because WAL mode raises the file format version numbers in the header from 1 to 2.

citations.quote: To prevent older versions of SQLite (prior to version 3.7.0, 2010-07-22) from trying to recover a WAL-mode database (and making matters worse) the database file format version numbers (bytes 18 and 19 in the database header) are increased from 1 to 2 in WAL mode.
A database in WAL journaling mode can only be accessed by SQLite version 3.7.0 (2010-07-21) or later.

facts.statement: WAL without shared memory works only if locking_mode is EXCLUSIVE before first access, and that connection then stays EXCLUSIVE until it leaves WAL mode.

citations.quote: In other words, a process can interact with a WAL database without using shared memory if that process is guaranteed to be the only process accessing the database.

In that case, the database connection remains in EXCLUSIVE mode as long as the journal mode is WAL; attempts to change the locking mode using "PRAGMA locking_mode=NORMAL;" are no-ops. The only way to change out of EXCLUSIVE locking mode is to first change out of WAL journal mode.

facts.statement: SQLite connections default to journal_mode=DELETE, and a database is converted to WAL by running PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL.

citations.quote: An SQLite database connection defaults to journal_mode=DELETE. To convert to WAL mode, use the following pragma:

PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;

The journal_mode pragma returns a string which is the new journal mode.

facts.statement: PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL returns "wal" on success; if conversion fails, for example because the VFS lacks shared-memory support, the mode is unchanged and the prior mode is returned.

citations.quote: On success, the pragma will return the string "wal". If the conversion to WAL could not be completed (for example, if the VFS does not support the necessary shared-memory primitives) then the journaling mode will be unchanged and the string returned from the primitive will be the prior journaling mode (for example "delete").

facts.statement: Unlike other journal modes, WAL mode is persistent: it stays in effect across connections and after the database is closed and reopened.

citations.quote: Unlike the other journaling modes, PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL is persistent. If a process sets WAL mode, then closes and reopens the database, the database will come back in WAL mode.
The WAL journaling mode is persistent; after being set it stays in effect across multiple database connections and after closing and reopening the database.

facts.statement: Non-WAL journal modes such as TRUNCATE do not persist; after closing and reopening, the database returns to the default DELETE rollback mode.

citations.quote: In contrast, if a process sets (for example) PRAGMA journal_mode=TRUNCATE and then closes and reopens the database will come back up in the default rollback mode of DELETE rather than the previous TRUNCATE setting.

facts.statement: Setting WAL journal mode on any one connection sets it on all connections to the same database file.

citations.quote: The WAL journal mode will be set on all connections to the same database file if it is set on any one connection.

facts.statement: Because WAL mode persists, an application can be switched to WAL without code changes by running PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL with a utility, then restarting the application.

citations.quote: The persistence of WAL mode means that applications can be converted to using SQLite in WAL mode without making any changes to the application itself. One has merely to run "PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;" on the database file(s) using the command-line shell or other utility, then restart the application.

facts.statement: PRAGMA journal_mode without a schema name changes the journal mode for all attached databases, and returns the original mode if the change could not be made.

citations.quote: The second form changes the journaling mode for "database" or for all attached databases if "database" is omitted. The new journal mode is returned. If the journal mode could not be changed, the original journal mode is returned.

facts.statement: The journal mode cannot be changed while a transaction is active, and in-memory databases can only use MEMORY or OFF, so they cannot use WAL.

citations.quote: Note that the journal_mode for an in-memory database is either MEMORY or OFF and can not be changed to a different value. An attempt to change the journal_mode of an in-memory database to any setting other than MEMORY or OFF is ignored. Note also that the journal_mode cannot be changed while a transaction is active.

facts.statement: Running PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE leaves WAL mode explicitly and changes the file format version numbers back to 1 so older SQLite versions can open the database.

citations.quote:
One can explicitly change out of WAL mode using a pragma such as this:

PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE;
Deliberately changing out of WAL mode changes the database file format version numbers back to 1 so that older versions of SQLite can once again access the database file.

facts.statement: When the last connection closes, it normally runs a final checkpoint and deletes the -wal and -shm files, though the WAL may remain after an unclean exit or with SQLITE_FCNTL_PERSIST_WAL.

citations.quote: When the last connection to a database closes, that connection does one last checkpoint and then deletes the WAL and its associated shared-memory file, to clean up the disk.

Usually, the WAL file is deleted automatically when the last connection to the database closes. However, if the last process to have the database open exits without cleanly shutting down the database connection, or if the SQLITE_FCNTL_PERSIST_WAL file control is used, then the WAL file might be retained on disk after all connections to the database have been closed.

facts.statement: If a connection is in EXCLUSIVE locking mode when first entering WAL mode, it cannot switch to NORMAL locking until it exits WAL mode; entering under NORMAL allows switching freely.

citations.quote: If the locking mode is EXCLUSIVE when first entering WAL journal mode, then the locking mode cannot be changed to NORMAL until after exiting WAL journal mode. If the locking mode is NORMAL when first entering WAL journal mode, then the locking mode can be changed between NORMAL and EXCLUSIVE and back again at any time and without needing to exit WAL journal mode.

facts.statement: Each SQLite WAL-mode read transaction fixes an "end mark" at the last valid commit record when it starts, so it sees the database as of a single point in time.

citations.quote: When a read operation begins on a WAL-mode database, it first remembers the location of the last valid commit record in the WAL. Call this point the "end mark". Because the WAL can be growing and adding new commit records while various readers connect to the database, each reader can potentially have its own end mark. But for any particular reader, the end mark is unchanged for the duration of the transaction, thus ensuring that a single read transaction only sees the database content as it existed at a single point in time.

facts.statement: A SQLite WAL-mode reader takes each page from the last WAL copy before its end mark, otherwise from the database file, using a shared-memory wal-index to locate pages.

citations.quote: When a reader needs a page of content, it first checks the WAL to see if that page appears there, and if so it pulls in the last copy of the page that occurs in the WAL prior to the reader's end mark. If no copy of the page exists in the WAL prior to the reader's end mark, then the page is read from the original database file.
a data structure called the "wal-index" is maintained in shared memory which helps readers locate pages in the WAL quickly and with a minimum of I/O.

facts.statement: SQLite WAL mode gives snapshot isolation: write transactions that commit while a read transaction is open stay invisible to that reader.

citations.quote: In WAL mode, SQLite exhibits "snapshot isolation". When a read transaction starts, that reader continues to see an unchanging "snapshot" of the database file as it existed at the moment in time when the read transaction started. Any write transactions that commit while the read transaction is active are still invisible to the read transaction, because the reader is seeing a snapshot of database file from a prior moment in time.

facts.statement: A SQLite connection holding a read transaction must end it and begin a new one, such as COMMIT then BEGIN, to see changes another connection committed meanwhile.

citations.quote: X can subsequently do a SELECT against the records that Y modified but X will see the older unmodified entries because Y's changes are all invisible to X while X is holding a read transaction. If X wants to see the changes that Y made, then X must end its read transaction and start a new one (by running COMMIT followed by another BEGIN.)
While its read transaction is active, X will continue to see an historic snapshot of the database prior to the changes implemented by Y.

facts.statement: SQLite readers on a separate connection never see a writer's uncommitted changes, unless both connections share a cache and the reader enables PRAGMA read_uncommitted.

citations.quote: then the reader is only able to see complete committed transactions from the writer. Partial changes by the writer that have not been committed are invisible to the reader.
The combined use of shared cache mode and the read_uncommitted pragma is the only way that one database connection can see uncommitted changes on a different database connection.

facts.statement: SQLite WAL mode's non-blocking behaviour has exceptions: queries can return SQLITE_BUSY when another connection uses exclusive locking mode, while the last connection cleans up, or during crash recovery.

citations.quote: The second advantage of WAL-mode is that writers do not block readers and readers do not block writers. This is mostly true. But there are some obscure cases where a query against a WAL-mode database can return SQLITE_BUSY, so applications should be prepared for that happenstance.
citations.locator: 9. Sometimes Queries Return SQLITE_BUSY In WAL Mode

citations.quote: If another database connection has the database mode open in exclusive locking mode then all queries against the database will return SQLITE_BUSY.
citations.locator: 9. Sometimes Queries Return SQLITE_BUSY In WAL Mode

citations.quote: When the last connection to a particular database is closing, that connection will acquire an exclusive lock for a short time while it cleans up the WAL and shared-memory files.
citations.locator: 9. Sometimes Queries Return SQLITE_BUSY In WAL Mode

citations.quote: If the last connection to a database crashed, then the first new connection to open the database will start a recovery process. An exclusive lock is held during recovery.
citations.locator: 9. Sometimes Queries Return SQLITE_BUSY In WAL Mode

facts.statement: SQLite returns the extended code SQLITE_BUSY_RECOVERY, only on WAL databases, when an operation cannot continue because another process is recovering the database after a crash.

citations.quote: The SQLITE_BUSY_RECOVERY error code is an extended error code for SQLITE_BUSY that indicates that an operation could not continue because another process is busy recovering a WAL mode database file following a crash. The SQLITE_BUSY_RECOVERY error code only occurs on WAL mode databases.

facts.statement: In SQLite WAL mode a checkpoint runs alongside readers but stops at pages past any current reader's end mark, so a long-running read transaction can stall checkpoint progress.

citations.quote: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.
Thus a long-running read transaction can prevent a checkpointer from making progress.

facts.statement: SQLite's manual SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE checkpoints run to completion, but readers might block while such a checkpoint runs.

citations.quote: In applications with many concurrent readers, one might also consider running manual checkpoints with the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART or SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE option which will ensure that the checkpoint runs to completion before returning. The disadvantage of using SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE is that readers might block while the checkpoint is running.

facts.statement: By contrast with WAL mode, SQLite rollback mode must temporarily expel all readers before a writer changes the database file on disk.

citations.quote: In rollback mode, SQLite implements isolation by locking the database file and preventing any reads by other database connections while each write transaction is underway.
But before any changes are made to the database file on disk, all readers must be (temporarily) expelled in order to give the writer exclusive access to the database file.

facts.statement: SQLite WAL mode allows only one writer at a time, because there is only one WAL file, although that writer runs alongside readers.

citations.quote: Writers merely append new content to the end of the WAL file. Because writers do nothing that would interfere with the actions of readers, writers and readers can run at the same time. However, since there is only one WAL file, there can only be one writer at a time.

facts.statement: SQLite supports multiple simultaneous read transactions from separate connections, threads or processes, but only one simultaneous write transaction.

citations.quote: SQLite supports multiple simultaneous read transactions coming from separate database connections, possibly in separate threads or processes, but only one simultaneous write transaction.

facts.statement: SQLite serializes writes: many open connections may write to the database, but they take turns, with locks applied automatically rather than by the application.

citations.quote: SQLite implements serializable transactions by actually serializing the writes. There can only be a single writer at a time to an SQLite database. There can be multiple database connections open at the same time, and all of those database connections can write to the database file, but they have to take turns. SQLite uses locks to serialize the writes automatically; this is not something that the applications using SQLite need to worry about.

facts.statement: When a second SQLite connection tries to start a write transaction while another write is underway, it gets SQLITE_BUSY and must wait for the first transaction to finish.

citations.quote: For example, if process A is in the middle of a large write transaction and at the same time process B attempts to start a new write transaction, process B will get back an SQLITE_BUSY result because SQLite only supports one writer at a time. Process B will need to wait for process A to finish its transaction before starting a new transaction.

facts.statement: SQLite offers sqlite3_busy_timeout(), sqlite3_busy_handler() and PRAGMA busy_timeout so a connection blocked by another writer can handle SQLITE_BUSY by waiting and retrying.

citations.quote: The sqlite3_busy_timeout() and sqlite3_busy_handler() interfaces and the busy_timeout pragma are available to process B to help it deal with SQLITE_BUSY errors.
If the callback returns non-zero, then another attempt is made to access the database and the cycle repeats.
citations.locator: Register A Callback To Handle SQLITE_BUSY Errors

facts.statement: SQLite's sqlite3_busy_timeout() handler sleeps repeatedly until at least the given number of milliseconds have accumulated, then lets sqlite3_step() return SQLITE_BUSY.

citations.quote: This routine sets a busy handler that sleeps for a specified amount of time when a table is locked. The handler will sleep multiple times until at least "ms" milliseconds of sleeping have accumulated. After at least "ms" milliseconds of sleeping, the handler returns 0 which causes sqlite3_step() to return SQLITE_BUSY.

facts.statement: SQLite's default busy callback is NULL, so unless a handler or timeout is set, a connection gets SQLITE_BUSY immediately when it meets a lock.

citations.quote: If the busy callback is NULL, then SQLITE_BUSY is returned immediately upon encountering the lock.
citations.locator: Register A Callback To Handle SQLITE_BUSY Errors

citations.quote: The default busy callback is NULL.
citations.locator: Register A Callback To Handle SQLITE_BUSY Errors

facts.statement: SQLite does not guarantee a busy handler runs: if invoking it could cause a deadlock, SQLite returns SQLITE_BUSY to the application instead.

citations.quote: The presence of a busy handler does not guarantee that it will be invoked when there is lock contention. If SQLite determines that invoking the busy handler could result in a deadlock, it will go ahead and return SQLITE_BUSY to the application instead of invoking the busy handler.
citations.locator: Register A Callback To Handle SQLITE_BUSY Errors

facts.statement: In SQLite WAL mode, a read transaction that tries to write after another connection has written fails with SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT and must release its snapshot and start a new transaction.

citations.quote: The attempt by X to escalate its transaction from a read transaction to a write transaction fails with an SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT error because the snapshot of the database being viewed by X is no longer the latest version of the database. If X were allowed to write, it would fork the history of the database file, which is something SQLite does not support. In order for X to write to the database, it must first release its snapshot (using ROLLBACK for example) then start a new transaction with a subsequent BEGIN.

The SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT error code is an extended error code for SQLITE_BUSY that occurs on WAL mode databases when a database connection tries to promote a read transaction into a write transaction but finds that another database connection has already written to the database and thus invalidated prior reads.

facts.statement: SQLite transactions default to DEFERRED, so one starting with SELECT is a read transaction whose later write upgrades it only if no other connection has modified or is modifying the database, otherwise SQLITE_BUSY.

citations.quote: Transactions can be DEFERRED, IMMEDIATE, or EXCLUSIVE. The default transaction behavior is DEFERRED.

If a write statement occurs while a read transaction is active, then the read transaction is upgraded to a write transaction if possible. If some other database connection has already modified the database or is already in the process of modifying the database, then upgrading to a write transaction is not possible and the write statement will fail with SQLITE_BUSY.

facts.statement: In SQLite WAL mode BEGIN EXCLUSIVE behaves the same as BEGIN IMMEDIATE; only in other journal modes does EXCLUSIVE also stop other connections reading.

citations.quote: EXCLUSIVE is similar to IMMEDIATE in that a write transaction is started immediately. EXCLUSIVE and IMMEDIATE are the same in WAL mode, but in other journaling modes, EXCLUSIVE prevents other database connections from reading the database while the transaction is underway.

facts.statement: A SQLite WAL checkpoint is the operation that moves transactions appended in the WAL file back into the original database file.

citations.quote: Of course, one wants to eventually transfer all the transactions that are appended in the WAL file back into the original database. Moving the WAL file transactions back into the database is called a "checkpoint".

facts.statement: By default, SQLite runs a checkpoint automatically whenever a COMMIT makes the WAL file 1000 pages or more, or when the last connection on the database file closes.

citations.quote: By default, SQLite will automatically checkpoint whenever a COMMIT occurs that causes the WAL file to be 1000 pages or more in size, or when the last database connection on a database file closes.

facts.statement: SQLite's default automatic checkpoint runs on the same thread as the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit, so occasional checkpoint-triggering COMMITs are much slower than most.

citations.quote: By default, the checkpoint will be run automatically by the same thread that does the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit. This has the effect of causing most COMMIT operations to be very fast but an occasional COMMIT (those that trigger a checkpoint) to be much slower.

facts.statement: Once the SQLite WAL reaches about 1000 pages, the default strategy runs a checkpoint for each subsequent COMMIT until the WAL is reset to fewer than 1000 pages.

citations.quote: The default strategy is to allow successive write transactions to grow the WAL until the WAL becomes about 1000 pages in size, then to run a checkpoint operation for each subsequent COMMIT until the WAL is reset to be smaller than 1000 pages.

facts.statement: SQLite's default automatic checkpoint threshold of 1000 pages can be changed at compile time with the SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT option.

citations.quote: By default, SQLite does a checkpoint automatically when the WAL file reaches a threshold size of 1000 pages. (The SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT compile-time option can be used to specify a different default.)

facts.statement: PRAGMA wal_autocheckpoint=N makes SQLite checkpoint automatically whenever the WAL equals or exceeds N pages, and setting it to zero or a negative value turns auto-checkpointing off.

citations.quote: This pragma queries or sets the write-ahead log auto-checkpoint interval. When the write-ahead log is enabled (via the journal_mode pragma) a checkpoint will be run automatically whenever the write-ahead log equals or exceeds N pages in length. Setting the auto-checkpoint size to zero or a negative value turns auto-checkpointing off.

facts.statement: SQLite's sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint() is a wrapper around sqlite3_wal_hook(), so registering a separate sqlite3_wal_hook() callback disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism.

citations.quote: The sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) is a wrapper around sqlite3_wal_hook() that causes any database on database connection D to automatically checkpoint after committing a transaction if there are N or more frames in the write-ahead log file.

The callback registered by this function replaces any existing callback registered using sqlite3_wal_hook(). Likewise, registering a callback using sqlite3_wal_hook() disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism configured by this function.

facts.statement: In SQLite, every new database connection starts with auto-checkpointing enabled at a threshold of 1000 pages, or the SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT value.

citations.quote: Every new database connection defaults to having the auto-checkpoint enabled with a threshold of 1000 or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT pages.

facts.statement: SQLite's automatic checkpoints are always PASSIVE: they do as much work as possible without interfering with other connections and might not run to completion when readers or writers are active.

citations.quote: The default checkpoint style is PASSIVE, which does as much work as it can without interfering with other database connections, and which might not run to completion if there are concurrent readers or writers. All checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() and by the automatic checkpoint mechanism are PASSIVE.
The busy-handler callback is never invoked in the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE mode. On the other hand, passive mode might leave the checkpoint unfinished if there are concurrent readers or writers.

facts.statement: Normally the SQLite WAL is checkpointed at about 1000 pages, about 4MB, and then recycled by overwriting it from the beginning rather than truncated, unless journal_size_limit is set.

citations.quote: In normal cases, new content is appended to the WAL file until the WAL file accumulates about 1000 pages (and is thus about 4MB in size) at which point a checkpoint is automatically run and the WAL file is recycled. The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set). Instead, it merely causes SQLite to start overwriting the WAL file from the beginning.

facts.statement: SQLite applications can force checkpoints with PRAGMA wal_checkpoint or sqlite3_wal_checkpoint(), or disable automatic checkpoints and run them during idle moments or in a separate thread or process.

citations.quote: Applications using WAL do not have to do anything in order for these checkpoints to occur. But if they want to, applications can adjust the automatic checkpoint threshold. Or they can turn off the automatic checkpoints and run checkpoints during idle moments or in a separate thread or process.
But programs that want more control can force a checkpoint using the wal_checkpoint pragma or by calling the sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() C interface.

facts.statement: A SQLite checkpoint can run alongside readers but must stop at any WAL page past a current reader's end mark, because continuing might overwrite database content that reader is using.

citations.quote: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader. The checkpoint has to stop at that point because otherwise it might overwrite part of the database file that the reader is actively using.

facts.statement: A SQLite checkpoint records its progress in the wal-index and resumes from there next time, so a long-running read transaction can stop the checkpointer from making progress.

citations.quote: The checkpoint remembers (in the wal-index) how far it got and will resume transferring content from the WAL to the database from where it left off on the next invocation.
Thus a long-running read transaction can prevent a checkpointer from making progress. But presumably every read transaction will eventually end and the checkpointer will be able to continue.

facts.statement: In SQLite checkpoint starvation, many overlapping readers keep at least one read transaction always active, so no checkpoint can complete or reset the WAL and the WAL file grows without bound.

citations.quote: Checkpoint starvation. A checkpoint is only able to run to completion, and reset the WAL file, if there are no other database connections using the WAL file. If another connection has a read transaction open, then the checkpoint cannot reset the WAL file because doing so might delete content out from under the reader.

However, if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

facts.statement: An unboundedly growing SQLite WAL file causes excess disk space usage and slow queries, because each reader must check the WAL and that time is proportional to the WAL file's size.

citations.quote: But it is possible to get SQLite into a state where the WAL file will grow without bound, causing excess disk space usage and slow query speeds.

On the other hand, read performance deteriorates as the WAL file grows in size since each reader must check the WAL file for the content and the time needed to check the WAL file is proportional to the size of the WAL file.

facts.statement: A SQLite WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction, so a very large write transaction can make the WAL grow very big until it completes.

citations.quote: Very large write transactions. A checkpoint can only complete when no other transactions are running, which means the WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction. So a large change to a large database might result in a large WAL file. The WAL file will be checkpointed once the write transaction completes (assuming there are no other readers blocking it) but in the meantime, the file can grow very big.

facts.statement: SQLite documentation says checkpoint starvation can be avoided by ensuring reader gaps, times when no process is reading the database, and attempting checkpoints during those gaps.

citations.quote: This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are "reader gaps": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.

facts.statement: Every SQLite checkpoint call needs an exclusive checkpoint lock, so a checkpoint attempted while another process is checkpointing returns SQLITE_BUSY without invoking the busy handler.

citations.quote: All calls obtain an exclusive "checkpoint" lock on the database file. If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned. Even if there is a busy-handler configured, it will not be invoked in this case.

facts.statement: If the busy handler returns 0 before a SQLite FULL, RESTART or TRUNCATE checkpoint gets the writer lock or while it waits for readers, it continues like PASSIVE and returns SQLITE_BUSY.

citations.quote: The SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, RESTART and TRUNCATE modes also obtain the exclusive "writer" lock on the database file.

If the busy-handler returns 0 before the writer lock is obtained or while waiting for database readers, the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE - checkpointing as many frames as possible without blocking any further. SQLITE_BUSY is returned in this case.

facts.statement: SQLite's PRAGMA wal_checkpoint returns 1 in its first column when a FULL, RESTART or TRUNCATE checkpoint was blocked from completing, for example by another thread or process using the database.

citations.quote: The wal_checkpoint pragma returns a single row with three integer columns. The first column is usually 0 but will be 1 if a RESTART or FULL or TRUNCATE checkpoint was blocked from completing, for example because another thread or process was actively using the database.

facts.statement: In SQLite WAL mode, synchronous=FULL syncs the WAL after every transaction commit, whereas synchronous=NORMAL omits that per-commit sync.

check.reason: Both quotes occur verbatim in wal.html section 2.3 and in the PRAGMA synchronous entry of pragma.html; they state FULL adds a WAL sync on each commit and NORMAL omits it.

citations.quote: (Writers sync the WAL on every transaction commit if PRAGMA synchronous is set to FULL but omit this sync if PRAGMA synchronous is set to NORMAL.)

With synchronous=FULL in WAL mode, an additional sync operation of the WAL file happens after each transaction commit. The extra WAL sync following each transaction helps ensure that transactions are durable across a power loss.

facts.statement: SQLite documents synchronous=FULL as atomic, consistent, isolated and durable (ACID) in WAL mode, unlike rollback-journal mode where FULL is not necessarily durable across power loss.

check.reason: Quote occurs in the FULL (2) item of PRAGMA synchronous; it says FULL is ACID in WAL mode and not necessarily durable across power loss in rollback mode.

citations.quote: FULL is atomic, consistent, isolated, and durable (ACID) in WAL mode and is atomic, consistent, and isolated with a rollback journal. FULL might also be durable using a rollback journal, depending on the underlying filesystem. FULL is not necessarily durable across a power loss in rollback mode

facts.statement: In SQLite WAL mode with synchronous=NORMAL, a committed transaction might roll back after a power loss or system crash, although the database stays consistent and safe from corruption.

check.reason: Quote occurs in the NORMAL (1) item; it says WAL with NORMAL is safe from corruption and always consistent, but a committed transaction might roll back after power loss or system crash.

citations.quote: WAL mode is safe from corruption with synchronous=NORMAL, and probably DELETE mode is safe too on modern filesystems. WAL mode is always consistent with synchronous=NORMAL, but WAL mode does lose durability. A transaction committed in WAL mode with synchronous=NORMAL might roll back following a power loss or system crash.

facts.statement: SQLite's pragma documentation calls synchronous=NORMAL the best performance-safety balance for most WAL-mode applications, losing only durability across power loss while keeping atomicity, consistency and isolation.

check.reason: Quote occurs in the NORMAL (1) item and supports the best-balance wording, the loss of durability across power loss and the retained atomicity, consistency and isolation.

citations.quote: The synchronous=NORMAL setting provides the best balance between performance and safety for most applications running in WAL mode. You lose durability across power lose with synchronous NORMAL in WAL mode, but that is not important for most applications. Transactions are still atomic, consistent, and isolated, which are the most important characteristics in most use cases.

facts.statement: In SQLite WAL mode with synchronous=NORMAL, syncs happen around checkpoints and WAL reuse, but no sync operations occur during most transactions.

check.reason: The pragma.html paragraph after the matrix lists the checkpoint and WAL-reuse syncs and says no sync occurs during most transactions; wal.html 2.3 agrees that the checkpoint is the only sync operation under NORMAL.

citations.quote: In WAL mode when synchronous is NORMAL (1), the WAL file is synchronized before each checkpoint and the database file is synchronized after each completed checkpoint and the WAL file header is synchronized when a WAL file begins to be reused after a checkpoint, but no sync operations occur during most transactions.
Note that with PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, the checkpoint is the only operation to issue an I/O barrier or sync operation (fsync() on unix or FlushFileBuffers() on windows).

facts.statement: SQLite says that with synchronous=NORMAL and checkpoints run in a separate thread or process, the main thread never blocks on sync, but transactions are no longer durable across power failure.

check.reason: In wal.html 2.3 the quoted sentences follow directly from the preceding sentence about synchronous=NORMAL ('therefore'), so the NORMAL condition, the never-blocking main thread and the loss of durability are all supported in context.

citations.quote: If an application therefore runs checkpoint in a separate thread or process, the main thread or process that is doing database queries and updates will never block on a sync operation. This helps to prevent "latch-up" in applications running on a busy disk drive.
