facts.statement: While another connection holds a SQLite read transaction open, a checkpoint does what it can but cannot run to completion or reset the WAL, and restarts where it left off after the next write transaction.

citations.quote: A checkpoint is only able to run to completion, and reset the WAL file, if there are no other database connections using the WAL file. If another connection has a read transaction open, then the checkpoint cannot reset the WAL file because doing so might delete content out from under the reader.

The checkpoint will do as much work as it can without upsetting the reader, but it cannot run to completion. The checkpoint will start up again where it left off after the next write transaction. This repeats until some checkpoint is able to complete.

facts.statement: SQLite's wal-index speeds finding pages in the WAL, but read performance still falls off as the WAL grows, so the documentation says to keep the WAL small by running checkpoints at regular intervals.

citations.quote: The wal-index helps find content in the WAL file much faster, but performance still falls off with increasing WAL file size. Hence, to maintain good read performance it is important to keep the WAL file size down by running checkpoints at regular intervals.

facts.statement: SQLite's automatic checkpoints are always PASSIVE, a mode that never invokes the busy handler and might leave the checkpoint unfinished when there are concurrent readers or writers.

citations.quote: Checkpoints initiated by this mechanism are PASSIVE.
This pragma is a wrapper around the sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint() C interface. All automatic checkpoints are PASSIVE.
The busy-handler callback is never invoked in the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE mode. On the other hand, passive mode might leave the checkpoint unfinished if there are concurrent readers or writers.

facts.statement: PRAGMA wal_checkpoint's second column reports modified pages written to the WAL and its third column the WAL pages moved back into the database by the checkpoint; both are -1 without a WAL.

citations.quote: The second column is the number of modified pages that have been written to the write-ahead log file. The third column is the number of pages in the write-ahead log file that have been successfully moved back into the database file at the conclusion of the checkpoint. The second and third column are -1 if there is no write-ahead log

facts.statement: sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() sets *pnLog to the total frames in the WAL and *pnCkpt to all checkpointed frames, including ones checkpointed before the call, or both to -1 on error or outside WAL mode.

citations.quote: The sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2(D,X,M,L,C) interface runs a checkpoint operation on database X of database connection D in mode M. Status information is written back into integers pointed to by L and C.

If pnLog is not NULL, then *pnLog is set to the total number of frames in the log file or to -1 if the checkpoint could not run because of an error or because the database is not in WAL mode. If pnCkpt is not NULL,then *pnCkpt is set to the total number of checkpointed frames in the log file (including any that were already checkpointed before the function was called) or to -1 if the checkpoint could not run due to an error or because the database is not in WAL mode.

facts.statement: SQLite's SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP mode always checkpoints zero frames and exists only to read the *pnLog and *pnCkpt values that sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() returns.

citations.quote: This mode always checkpoints zero frames. The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() via output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt.

facts.statement: A SQLite RESTART checkpoint works like FULL but also waits, via the busy handler, until all readers read only from the database file, so the next writer restarts the WAL from the beginning; TRUNCATE also truncates it to zero bytes.

citations.quote: This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL with the addition that after checkpointing the log file it blocks (calls the busy-handler callback) until all readers are reading from the database file only. This ensures that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning.
This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.

facts.statement: sqlite3_busy_timeout installs a busy handler that sleeps until at least the given milliseconds accumulate and then returns 0, the value that makes a blocking SQLite checkpoint fall back to PASSIVE behaviour.

citations.quote: This routine sets a busy handler that sleeps for a specified amount of time when a table is locked. The handler will sleep multiple times until at least "ms" milliseconds of sleeping have accumulated. After at least "ms" milliseconds of sleeping, the handler returns 0 which causes sqlite3_step() to return SQLITE_BUSY.

If the busy-handler returns 0 before the writer lock is obtained or while waiting for database readers, the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE - checkpointing as many frames as possible without blocking any further.

facts.statement: A SQLite checkpoint normally only overwrites the WAL from the beginning rather than truncating it; journal_size_limit truncates a larger leftover WAL at each commit or WAL reset, default -1 meaning no limit.

citations.quote: The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set). Instead, it merely causes SQLite to start overwriting the WAL file from the beginning.

Each time a transaction is committed or a WAL file resets, SQLite compares the size of the rollback journal file or WAL file left in the file-system to the size limit set by this pragma and if the journal or WAL file is larger it is truncated to the limit.
The default journal size limit is -1 (no limit).

facts.statement: SQLite compile-time option SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT sets the default auto-checkpoint page count, otherwise 1000, and SQLITE_DEFAULT_JOURNAL_SIZE_LIMIT sets the WAL size limit, otherwise unbounded.

citations.quote: This macro sets the default page count for the WAL automatic checkpointing feature. If unspecified, the default page count is 1000.

This option sets the size limit on rollback journal files in persistent journal mode and exclusive locking mode or sets the size of the write-ahead log file in WAL mode. When this compile-time option is omitted there is no upper bound on the size of the rollback journals or write-ahead logs.

facts.statement: SQLite's sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) checkpoints after a commit once the WAL has N or more frames, and passing zero or a negative N disables automatic checkpoints entirely.

citations.quote: The sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) is a wrapper around sqlite3_wal_hook() that causes any database on database connection D to automatically checkpoint after committing a transaction if there are N or more frames in the write-ahead log file. Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.

facts.statement: A sqlite3_wal_hook callback receives the number of pages currently in the WAL, including those just committed, and an application that sets one should periodically checkpoint to keep the WAL from growing without bound.

check.reason: The cited quotes do not state that the callback runs after each commit; that wording comes from uncited text on the page, so the statement is limited to what the quoted passages say.

citations.quote: The fourth parameter is the number of pages currently in the write-ahead log file, including those that were just committed.

If a write-ahead log callback is set using this function then sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() or PRAGMA wal_checkpoint should be invoked periodically to keep the write-ahead log file from growing without bound.

facts.original_statement: A sqlite3_wal_hook callback runs after each SQLite WAL commit, receiving the number of pages currently in the WAL, and an application using one should checkpoint periodically to stop unbounded WAL growth.

original.statement: SQLite says the only safe way to remove a leftover WAL file is to open the database with an sqlite3_open() interface and then immediately close it with sqlite3_close().

citations.quote: The only safe way to remove a WAL file is to open the database file using one of the sqlite3_open() interfaces then immediately close the database using sqlite3_close().

aliases.reason: Both say, from the same wal.html passage, that the only safe way to remove a WAL file is to open the database with sqlite3_open() and immediately close it.

original.statement: Because the WAL cannot be reset during a write transaction, a large change to a large database can make the WAL file grow very big until the transaction completes.

citations.quote: Very large write transactions. A checkpoint can only complete when no other transactions are running, which means the WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction. So a large change to a large database might result in a large WAL file. The WAL file will be checkpointed once the write transaction completes (assuming there are no other readers blocking it) but in the meantime, the file can grow very big.

aliases.reason: Both say, from the same wal.html passage, that the WAL cannot be reset during a write transaction, so a very large write transaction can make it grow very large.

previous.statement: SQLite's network guidance names a client/server database such as PostgreSQL, or SQLite in rollback mode, as the other choices when multiple machines access one database.

citations.quote: Use a client/server database engine. PostgreSQL is an excellent choice. A variation of this is:
Use SQLite in rollback mode. This means you can have multiple simultaneous readers or one writer, but not simultaneous readers and writers.

revisions.reason: The useovernet.html Recommendations list applies to multiple clients on different machines that need simultaneous reads and writes, not to any multi-machine access, and the quoted rollback-mode option itself says it allows multiple simultaneous readers or one writer but not simultaneous readers and writers; the statement is narrowed to that context and caveat.

previous.statement: WAL documentation says WAL works best with smaller transactions and once recommended rollback modes above about 100 megabytes, but since version 3.11.0 WAL handles large transactions as efficiently as rollback mode.

citations.quote: WAL works best with smaller transactions. WAL does not work well for very large transactions. For transactions larger than about 100 megabytes, traditional rollback journal modes will likely be faster. For transactions in excess of a gigabyte, WAL mode may fail with an I/O or disk-full error. It is recommended that one of the rollback journal modes be used for transactions larger than a few dozen megabytes. Beginning with version 3.11.0 (2016-02-15), WAL mode works as efficiently with large transactions as does rollback mode.

revisions.reason: In the original Overview paragraph about 100 megabytes is where rollback modes 'will likely be faster', while the recommendation threshold is 'a few dozen megabytes'; the statement conflated the two. The page also presents this advice in the present tense, not as something it 'once' said, alongside the 3.11.0 sentence, without reconciling them.

previous.statement: The WAL file is part of the database's persistent state and must be copied or moved with it; separating them can lose committed transactions or corrupt the database.

citations.quote: The WAL file is part of the persistent state of the database and should be kept with the database if the database is copied or moved. If a database file is separated from its WAL file, then transactions that were previously committed to the database might be lost, or the database file might become corrupted.

revisions.reason: Section 4 says the WAL file 'should be kept with the database' if copied or moved, and that separation 'might' lose committed transactions or corrupt the file; 'must' and 'can' overstated the modality.

previous.statement: In SQLite WAL mode, readers do not block writers and a writer does not block readers, so reading and writing can proceed concurrently.

citations.quote: WAL provides more concurrency as readers do not block writers and a writer does not block readers. Reading and writing can proceed concurrently.
WAL mode permits simultaneous readers and writers. It can do this because changes do not overwrite the original database file, but rather go into the separate write-ahead log file.

revisions.reason: Both quotes occur in the originals under the cited headings and state the general property, but section 9 of the same wal.html page says this is only 'mostly true' and lists obscure cases returning SQLITE_BUSY, and section 6 says readers might block during RESTART/TRUNCATE checkpoints, so the unqualified wording overstates the source.

previous.statement: SQLite WAL mode lets readers keep using the unaltered database file during a write, because a COMMIT only appends a commit record to the separate WAL file.

citations.quote: The original content is preserved in the database file and the changes are appended into a separate WAL file. A COMMIT occurs when a special record indicating a commit is appended to the WAL. Thus a COMMIT can happen without ever writing to the original database, which allows readers to continue operating from the original unaltered database while changes are simultaneously being committed into the WAL.

revisions.reason: The quote (wal.html, 2. How WAL Works) says the changes themselves are appended to the WAL and a COMMIT occurs when a commit record is appended, so a COMMIT 'can happen without ever writing' the database; 'a COMMIT only appends a commit record' understates what is written to the WAL, and section 2.3 notes an automatic checkpoint can run in the committing thread, so the wording follows the source's 'can happen without'.

previous.statement: SQLite BEGIN IMMEDIATE starts a write transaction at once, blocking other writers; it may fail with SQLITE_BUSY, but once it succeeds later statements in it never fail with SQLITE_BUSY.

citations.quote: IMMEDIATE causes the database connection to start a new write immediately, without waiting for a write statement. The BEGIN IMMEDIATE might fail with SQLITE_BUSY if another write transaction is already active on another database connection.

The BEGIN IMMEDIATE command goes ahead and starts a write transaction, and thus blocks all other writers. If the BEGIN IMMEDIATE operation succeeds, then no subsequent operations in that transaction will ever fail with an SQLITE_BUSY error.

revisions.reason: Both quotes occur as cited, but the no-later-SQLITE_BUSY guarantee is quoted from the WAL-mode discussion in isolation.html, while lang_transaction.html section 2.3 says COMMIT can return SQLITE_BUSY if another thread or process has an open read connection; the documentation is not consistent on this outside WAL mode, so the claim is restricted to WAL mode, which the cited context supports.

previous.statement: SQLite's FULL checkpoint waits for no writer and all readers on the latest snapshot, then checkpoints every frame; RESTART also waits until readers leave the log, and TRUNCATE also truncates it to zero bytes.

citations.quote: This mode blocks (it invokes the busy-handler callback) until there is no database writer and all readers are reading from the most recent database snapshot. It then checkpoints all frames in the log file and syncs the database file. This mode blocks new database writers while it is pending, but new database readers are allowed to continue unimpeded.

This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL with the addition that after checkpointing the log file it blocks (calls the busy-handler callback) until all readers are reading from the database file only. This ensures that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning.
This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.

revisions.reason: The C API page says the waiting is done through the busy-handler callback and that TRUNCATE truncates the log 'just prior to a successful return'; the original wording made the wait and the truncation sound unconditional, while the same page says a busy handler returning 0 makes these modes fall back to PASSIVE behaviour.

previous.statement: A SQLite writer rewinds the WAL to its beginning only when the entire WAL has been transferred into the database and synced and no readers are using the WAL.

citations.quote: Whenever a write operation occurs, the writer checks how much progress the checkpointer has made, and if the entire WAL has been transferred into the database and synced and if no readers are making use of the WAL, then the writer will rewind the WAL back to the beginning and start putting new transactions at the beginning of the WAL. This mechanism prevents a WAL file from growing without bound.

revisions.reason: The cited passage in section 2.2 states these as the conditions under which the writer rewinds ('if ... then the writer will rewind'), not as the only conditions; 'only when' is stronger than the quoted text.

previous.statement: If a SQLite application disables or defers the automatic checkpoint through compile-time or run-time options, nothing prevents the WAL file from growing excessively.

citations.quote: However, compile-time and run-time options exist that can disable or defer this automatic checkpoint. If an application disables the automatic checkpoint, then there is nothing to prevent the WAL file from growing excessively.

revisions.reason: Section 6 says nothing prevents excessive WAL growth only for an application that disables the automatic checkpoint; it does not say this of options that merely defer it.

previous.statement: With many concurrent SQLite readers, manual RESTART or TRUNCATE checkpoints ensure the checkpoint runs to completion before returning, at the cost that readers might block while it runs.

citations.quote: In applications with many concurrent readers, one might also consider running manual checkpoints with the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART or SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE option which will ensure that the checkpoint runs to completion before returning. The disadvantage of using SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE is that readers might block while the checkpoint is running.

revisions.reason: The WAL page offers this as something 'one might also consider'; it is attributed rather than asserted because the sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2 page says these modes fall back to PASSIVE and return SQLITE_BUSY if the busy handler returns 0, and describes RESTART as not impeding readers, so completion and reader blocking are the WAL page's own characterisation.

previous.statement: SQLite's built-in default synchronous setting is FULL, and WAL-mode databases keep that default unless SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_SYNCHRONOUS is overridden at compile time.

citations.quote: This macro determines the default value of the PRAGMA synchronous setting. If not overridden at compile-time, the default setting is 2 (FULL).

This macro determines the default value of the PRAGMA synchronous setting for database files that open in WAL mode. If not overridden at compile-time, this value is the same as SQLITE_DEFAULT_SYNCHRONOUS.

revisions.reason: compile.html section 4 ties the WAL-mode default to SQLITE_DEFAULT_SYNCHRONOUS, which can itself be overridden; the source does not say WAL databases stay at FULL whenever only SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_SYNCHRONOUS is left alone.

previous.statement: SQLite says WAL makes disk I/O more sequential and uses many fewer fsync() operations than a rollback journal, making it less vulnerable on systems where fsync() is broken.

citations.quote: Disk I/O operations tends to be more sequential using WAL.
WAL uses many fewer fsync() operations and is thus less vulnerable to problems on systems where the fsync() system call is broken.

revisions.reason: wal.html section 1 hedges that disk I/O 'tends to be' more sequential using WAL; the original statement said WAL 'makes' disk I/O more sequential, which is stronger than the source.

previous.statement: SQLite's WAL page warns that transactions over a gigabyte may fail in WAL mode with an I/O or disk-full error, while noting WAL handles large transactions as efficiently as rollback mode since version 3.11.0.

citations.quote: For transactions in excess of a gigabyte, WAL mode may fail with an I/O or disk-full error. It is recommended that one of the rollback journal modes be used for transactions larger than a few dozen megabytes. Beginning with version 3.11.0 (2016-02-15), WAL mode works as efficiently with large transactions as does rollback mode.

revisions.reason: On the live wal.html (last updated 2026-08-25), the text from 'WAL works best with smaller transactions' through 'transactions larger than a few dozen megabytes', including the gigabyte I/O or disk-full warning, is wrapped in <s> strikethrough markup as superseded; only the version 3.11.0 sentence is current. The pinned extraction drops the strikethrough, so presenting the gigabyte failure as a current warning is not supported.

previous.statement: For an SQLite database used by one process, EXCLUSIVE locking mode reduces filesystem system calls, possibly a small performance gain, and in WAL mode allocates the wal-index from heap instead of a -shm file.

citations.quote: The number of system calls for filesystem operations is reduced, possibly resulting in a small performance increase.

For example, if PRAGMA locking_mode is set to EXCLUSIVE (meaning that only one process is able to access the database file) then the shared memory will be allocated from heap rather than out of the shared-memory file, and the shared-memory file will never be created.

revisions.reason: Both quotes occur (pragma.html PRAGMA locking_mode; tempfiles.html 2.3 Shared-Memory Files), but wal.html section 8 says the heap wal-index is used only when EXCLUSIVE is set before the first WAL-mode database access, so the unconditional claim is attributed and softened. The system-call reduction is a general EXCLUSIVE-mode benefit, not a WAL-versus-rollback comparison.

previous.statement: A sqlite3_wal_hook callback runs after each SQLite WAL commit, receiving the number of pages currently in the WAL, and an application using one should checkpoint periodically to stop unbounded WAL growth.

citations.quote: The fourth parameter is the number of pages currently in the write-ahead log file, including those that were just committed.

If a write-ahead log callback is set using this function then sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() or PRAGMA wal_checkpoint should be invoked periodically to keep the write-ahead log file from growing without bound.

revisions.reason: The cited quotes do not state that the callback runs after each commit; that wording comes from uncited text on the page, so the statement is limited to what the quoted passages say.

gaps.question: sync-durability
gaps.reason: The sqlite.org pages inspected say only that recent commits might roll back under synchronous=NORMAL after power loss; they do not quantify how many transactions or how much time can be lost.

gaps.question: other-limits
gaps.reason: Checker assessment: the WAL page's large-transaction limits (rollback likely faster above about 100 MB, recommended above a few dozen MB, possible I/O or disk-full failure above a gigabyte) sit beside its statement that WAL has handled large transactions as efficiently as rollback mode since 3.11.0 (2016-02-15); no inspected source says which of these limits still apply to current releases.

gaps.question: gap-question-1
gaps.reason: Checker's assessment: the checked facts omit two performance caveats documented in wal.html section 2.3. The default automatic checkpoint makes most COMMITs very fast but an occasional COMMIT (one that triggers a checkpoint) much slower. Running checkpoints in a separate thread under synchronous=NORMAL means transactions are no longer durable and might roll back after a power failure or hard reset. The old large-transaction warning is struck through on the current page, so no current large-transaction disadvantage is documented.

gaps.question: checkpoint-starvation
gaps.reason: The sqlite.org pages inspected describe no dedicated starvation alarm, threshold or interface identifying which reader blocks a checkpoint; detection has to rely on checkpoint return codes, log and checkpointed frame counts, and WAL size.

conflicts.note: wal.html presents RESTART and TRUNCATE checkpoints as running to completion, while the sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() page says FULL, RESTART and TRUNCATE continue like PASSIVE and return SQLITE_BUSY if the busy handler gives up, so completion is not guaranteed.
